etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English comen, cumen, from Old English cuman, from Proto-West Germanic *kweman, from Proto-Germanic *kwemaną (“to come”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷémt (“to step”), from *gʷem- (“to step”).

definitions.definition: To move toward the speaker.
To move toward the listener.
To move toward the object that is the focus of the sentence.
(in subordinate clauses and gerunds) To move toward the agent or subject of the main clause.
To move toward an unstated agent.
(intransitive) To move nearer to the point of perspective.

definitions.definition: (typography, obsolete) Alternative form of comma in its medieval use as a middot ⟨·⟩ serving as a form of colon.

quote.citation: 1824, J. Johnson, Typographia:
quote.text: There be five manner of points and divisions most used among cunning men; the which if they be well used, make the sentence very light and easy to be understood, both to the reader and hearer: and they be these, virgil,—come,—parenthesis,—plain point,—interrogative.

quote.citation: 1842, F. Francillon, An Essay on Punctuation‎[5], page 9:
quote.text: Whoever introduced the several points, it seems that a full-point, a point called come, answering to our colon-point, a point called virgil answering to our comma-point, the parenthesis-points and interrogative-point, were used at the close of the fourteenth, or beginning of the fifteenth century.
